title: Pool Equipment and Plumbing Leaks That Reach the House | Gold Water Fire, Phoenix, AZ
description: Why pool pad leaks and buried pool plumbing end up as damp drywall, warped floors and musty rooms inside Phoenix homes, and how to trace the source.
h1: When Pool Equipment & Plumbing Leaks Find Their Way Into the House
breadcrumbLabel: Pool Equipment Leaks Into the Home
intro: You have been filling the pool more than you used to. Not dramatically, just often enough that you noticed, and then stopped noticing, and then noticed again. There is a patch of baseboard in the back bedroom that feels cool to the touch. The tile in the hallway sounds different underfoot in one spot. Maybe a smell shows up in the afternoon and is gone by morning. None of it is big enough to be an emergency, and that is exactly what makes it hard to sit with. You have looked under sinks. You have checked the water heater. Nothing is dripping anywhere you can see, and yet something is clearly happening, and it has probably been happening for a while. That gap between knowing something is wrong and being able to point at it is its own kind of tiring.

sections.heading: A pool leak does not behave like a plumbing leak
sections.body:
Most homeowners are trained to look for leaks the way they show up in movies: a burst pipe, water on the floor, an obvious source. Pool systems almost never fail that way. The equipment pad sits outside, often on the far side of the house, and the plumbing that feeds it runs underground through soil, under concrete decking, and sometimes under the slab edge of the house itself. Water that escapes there has nowhere dramatic to go. It soaks into dirt. It travels along the path of least resistance, which in Arizona is very often the trench line that was dug when the pool was installed, or the sand and gravel bed under a patio. By the time it reaches the house, it is not a stream. It is saturated soil pressing against a footing, and moisture wicking up through concrete into the bottom few inches of drywall.

That is why the symptoms feel disconnected from the cause. The damage shows up in a room, and the failure is thirty feet away in a pipe you have never seen. Evaporation makes it worse: in the dry heat here, a pool loses water naturally, so a real leak can hide inside what you assume is normal summer loss for months.

sections.heading: The specific parts that let go, and what each one looks like
sections.body: Pool water systems have a handful of predictable failure points. Knowing which one you are looking at changes how the water moves and where it ends up.

cards.heading: Pump and filter connections at the pad
cards.body: Threaded unions, pump seals and filter clamp bands are the most common drips. Sun and heat make PVC brittle and dry out O-rings. The giveaway is a permanently damp or stained patch of concrete under the equipment, or efflorescence (white crusty mineral deposits) on the pad. If the pad sits against an exterior wall of the house, that constant wet spot can push moisture straight through the wall into the room behind it. Run the pump and look, then shut it off and look again; suction-side leaks often only weep when the system is off, and pressure-side leaks spray only when it is running.

cards.heading: Buried suction and return lines
cards.body: The pipes running between the pool and the pad are underground. A cracked return line leaks only when the pump runs and can move a lot of water quietly. A classic sign is a soft, sunken or unusually green strip of yard tracing a straight line from the pool toward the equipment, or decking that has settled and cracked along that same line.

cards.heading: Skimmer throats and light conduit
cards.body: The skimmer is a plastic box set in concrete, and the joint where it meets the pool shell cracks with ground movement. Water leaving there goes directly into the soil beside the pool. Pool light conduit can also carry water back toward a junction box near the house. Both leak at a fixed level, so a pool that drops and then stops at a consistent line is telling you where the hole is.

cards.heading: Autofill lines and backwash runs
cards.body: The autofill valve is fed by house plumbing, usually a small line trenched from the home. That line is easy to nick and can leak continuously without anyone noticing, because the pool level always looks fine. Backwash and drain lines that discharge too close to the foundation cause the same result over time: repeated soaking of the soil right against the house.

sections.heading: What outside water looks like once it is indoors
sections.body:
Moisture entering from below and from the outside edge announces itself differently than a supply line break. Watch the bottom of the wall, not the middle. Baseboards that swell, cup or separate slightly from the drywall. Paint that bubbles in a band a few inches off the floor. Carpet that stays cool and slightly heavy near an exterior wall while the rest of the room is dry. Wood or laminate flooring that peaks at the seams. Tile that sounds hollow when tapped because the thinset bond is releasing. A musty smell that is strongest low and near that wall, and that comes back after you air the room out.

Drywall wicks water upward, so what you see is always lower and smaller than what is actually wet. Insulation inside the wall cavity holds moisture long after the surface feels dry, and the back side of the drywall, plus the bottom plate of the framing, can stay damp for weeks. In Phoenix homes with post-tension slabs and stucco exteriors, water that gets under the stucco weep screed or behind a patio slab poured too high against the wall has a hard time getting back out.

The reason this matters is timing. Mold growth needs moisture and time, not a flood. A wall that stays at elevated moisture from a slow outdoor leak has both. Drying it properly means finding and stopping the source first, because equipment that removes moisture cannot outrun a pipe that is still leaking.

sections.heading: Narrowing it down before anyone opens a wall
sections.body: You can do a fair amount of this yourself, and it is worth doing, because it tells whoever comes out where to start. Start with the bucket test. Fill a bucket with pool water, set it on a step so the water inside the bucket and the pool water outside it are at the same level, mark both lines, and leave the pump running normally for 24 hours. Evaporation affects both equally. If the pool drops more than the bucket, you have a leak. Repeat with the pump off; a bigger drop with the pump running points to pressure-side return plumbing, while a bigger drop with the pump off points to the suction side or the pool shell. Then look for the physical tells: settled decking, a wet or algae-streaked line in the yard, a damp equipment pad that never dries, mineral staining on stucco near the pad, and soil that stays dark next to the foundation. Turn off the autofill valve for a day and watch what the level actually does without it masking the loss. When a leak has been running long enough to reach interior finishes, the two problems separate: the pool side needs a leak detection and repair specialist, and the building side needs the wet materials found, dried and, where they cannot be saved, removed and rebuilt. Those are different trades. On the building side, the work is water damage restoration, and if drywall, baseboard, flooring or cabinetry has to come out, putting the room back is reconstruction and rebuild work. If you want a set of eyes on what the water has done inside the house, you can reach out and describe what you are seeing.

faqs.q: How much water loss is normal for a pool in the Phoenix area?
faqs.a: Evaporation is real here, especially in summer heat and wind, so some loss is expected in any uncovered pool. Rather than guessing at a number, use the bucket test: a bucket of pool water sitting on a step evaporates at the same rate as the pool. If the pool level falls faster than the water in the bucket, the difference is a leak, not evaporation.

faqs.q: Can a pool leak really damage the inside of my house?
faqs.a: Yes, though usually slowly. Underground pool plumbing and a wet equipment pad saturate the soil, and that moisture can move along trench lines and under decking until it reaches the foundation. From there it wicks up into the bottom of drywall, baseboards and flooring. The interior damage often shows up months after the leak started, which is why the two rarely get connected right away.

faqs.q: Do I have to fix the pool leak before drying out the house?
faqs.a: The source has to be stopped first, or at least isolated, before drying can finish. Dehumidifiers and air movers pull existing moisture out of materials, but they cannot keep up with water that is still arriving. In practice you can shut the pump down or valve off the suspect line to stop the flow while repairs are scheduled, and drying can begin at that point.

faqs.q: Will homeowners insurance cover this kind of damage?
faqs.a: It depends on the policy and on how the loss is classified, and that is a question for your carrier or adjuster. Generally, gradual seepage is treated differently than a sudden failure, and the cost to repair the pool plumbing itself is often handled separately from damage to the house. Documenting what you find with photos and dates before anything is torn out helps either way.
